title: Availability Outruns Selection
question: Why can a larger candidate pool contain better answers without improving the answer returned?

steps.title: Separate availability from selection

steps.title: More available answers do not force better votes
steps.description: Coverage continues climbing while majority voting flattens. A selector returning an unchanged pool member cannot exploit a correct candidate it fails to recognize.

steps.title: Give the selector usable evidence
steps.description: The dotted repair curve measures coverage under tests. Its availability is useful only insofar as the tests identify candidates satisfying their tested predicate, which remains narrower than complete task acceptance.

steps.title: Compare on the recorded sample range
steps.description: The pool-size axis is logarithmic. The repair series ends much earlier than the mathematical series; the absent continuation is not an invitation to extrapolate it.

title: Stopping Precedence

scope: Stopping search does not make the acceptance decision. Hard ceilings stop new admissions even if further work appears valuable.

title: The tool-call loop
question: How does one model turn become bounded observations without dispatching invalid or unauthorized calls?
scope: The diagram separates pre-dispatch rejection from effect tracking. A dispatched operation with an unknown effect must remain unknown in its observation.

steps.title: Identify every proposal

steps.title: Reject before dispatch when required
steps.description: Schema validation rejects call_3, and authorization rejects call_2. Their error observations return without claiming any tool effect occurred.

steps.title: Track the dispatched call
steps.description: Only the permitted call reaches the tool or environment. Dispatch must track the available outcome; sending a request alone does not prove completion.

steps.title: Return bounded, correlated observations
steps.description: Shape bounds the tool return and matches its call ID. The next turn receives call_1’s result and the two rejection errors, preserving each proposal’s identity.

title: Bounded capture before staging
question: How can a tool adapter drain an arbitrarily long output stream while keeping capture memory bounded?
scope: Capture and staged-observation budgets count bytes, while the next model call is measured in tokens. Raw-record retention and later range reads require authorization.

steps.title: Drain both channels under limits
steps.description: One readiness loop drains stdout and stderr, enforcing a byte limit and deadline. Draining both pipes prevents one full channel from stalling the child process.

steps.title: Keep a fixed head and rolling tail
steps.description: The head fills once. The tail ring replaces its oldest bytes as new output arrives, so longer output does not require a larger capture buffer.

steps.title: Count the missing middle honestly
steps.description: Middle bytes are counted without being kept in capture memory. The omission notice describes that measured gap rather than pretending the staged output is complete.

steps.title: Stage a bounded observation
steps.description: Status, head, omission notice, tail, and a handle form the observation. The model’s token budget is a separate constraint from this byte budget.

steps.title: Retrieve ranges only when permitted
steps.description: An authorized retained record may support later range reads by handle. That optional store is separate from the fixed-size capture buffers.

title: Collection Credits Across Four Responsibilities
question: When can a collection run return its credit to the admission pool?
scope: A credit bounds unsettled collection responsibility, not just active rollout execution. Feedback delay never overrides the hard admission limit.

pool.label: Credit pool, watermark, and hard limit

steps.title: Reserve capacity before rollout
steps.description: Admission acquires a credit from the pool. The watermark slows dispatch as in-flight work rises, while the hard limit stops admission if feedback arrives too late.

steps.title: Carry responsibility through assessment
steps.description: The same admitted run keeps its credit through rollout, capture, staging, and assessment. Finishing model execution does not free capacity still needed for the record.

steps.title: Wait for a durable destination
steps.description: The record reaches dataset publication, a diagnostic pool, or an unresolved review queue. Transfer to another owner releases responsibility only when that bounded owner acknowledges it.

steps.title: Return the credit only at the boundary
steps.description: The dashed return path begins after durable disposition or acknowledged transfer. This keeps capture and assessment backlogs inside the collection capacity bound.

title: A Derived Record and Its Lineage
question: What must a redacted trajectory preserve before it can be admitted for learning?
scope: Lineage does not authorize reading restricted raw data, and retaining a hash is not retaining the source. A transformed view must be revalidated for its declared use.

steps.title: Create a new version
steps.description: Redaction produces a distinct derived record instead of editing trace_r19_01 in place. The versioned transformation records the changed fields and omissions.

steps.title: Retain lineage and partition boundaries
steps.description: The derived record links to its parent and keeps the same split group. Those references preserve provenance and evaluation separation without granting raw-source access.

steps.title: Revalidate the transformed evidence
steps.description: The derived assessment is pending. Removing fields can remove the evidence for a target, so revalidation decides which declared use remains supported or must be withheld.

steps.title: Propagate later corrections
steps.description: The source’s reverse reference reaches the derived version for correction or withdrawal. Provenance must work in both directions after transformation.

title: Cost per Trial Barely Tracks Score
question: How much does trial price reveal about a long-horizon configuration’s score and repeatability?
scope: Points are observed configuration means over five trials. Vertical bars are observed worst-to-best ranges, not confidence intervals, and score is not an acceptance probability.

steps.title: Read a configuration, not a purchase guarantee
steps.description: Each dot is a configuration’s mean score, and parenthesized labels show average trial hours. The horizontal axis measures the average cost of one trial on a logarithmic scale.

steps.title: Compare scores at similar prices
steps.description: The middle cost band contains configurations with widely separated mean scores. Spending a similar amount does not imply obtaining a similar result.

steps.title: Retain the variation across trials
steps.description: The light bars span the worst and best of five trials. Their overlap and width show observed variability; they are not statistical confidence intervals around the means.

steps.title: Assess the expensive increment
steps.description: The far-right labeled configuration has the highest mean, while near-leading means appear much farther left. This measured comparison motivates routing analysis without proving that a price increase causes a score increase.

title: A Gated Three-Tier Cascade
question: How does a cascade lower cost per accepted result while charging unsuccessful attempts?
scope: Prices and acceptance rates are stipulated workload inputs. The direct-frontier cohort is a separate baseline, and accepted gate verdicts are not proof of every operational property.

steps.title: Charge the initial cohort’s gate
steps.description: All initiated tasks reach tier one and its assessment. The passing portion exits to accepted outcomes; only the rejected remainder moves downward.

steps.title: Pay for every reached attempt
steps.description: Tier two and tier three each charge their call and gate to the tasks that reach them. Earlier failed attempts stay in total cohort cost when a later tier succeeds.

steps.title: Keep unresolved tasks visible
steps.description: The final gate still charges its assessment. Its rejected sliver remains unresolved rather than being folded into accepted outcomes.

steps.title: Divide by accepted results, not initiated tasks
steps.description: The lower bars charge all attempts to the accepted outcomes. Compare this with the separately stipulated direct-frontier cohort, rather than applying the last tier’s conditional acceptance to every initial task.
